summary: Records the deprecation of IKEv1 and updates guidance on older algorithms tied to it that are not commonly used with IKEv2. It also adds a Status column to the IKEv2 Transform Type Values registries.

eli5.summary: The old key-setup method is retired, and old tools that went with it are marked as no longer recommended.

subtitle: IKEv1 is retired for good, and a batch of old, unused algorithms are marked deprecated in the IKEv2 registries.

tldr.problem: IKEv1 was replaced by IKEv2 long ago but still lingers in unmaintained code, and many aged algorithms were left in a vague 'MAY be used' state because RFCs 8221 and 8247 never mentioned them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC declares IKEv1 and its related documents Historic, lists the IKEv1 features that now have IKEv2 equivalents, deprecates the unmentioned old algorithms, and adds a Status column to the IKEv2 Transform Type registries.
tldr.outcome: Systems that only speak IKEv1 should be upgraded or replaced, and the deprecated algorithm names are now flagged DEPRECATED in IANA's IKEv2 registries.

today: RFC 9395 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2023. It updates RFC 8221 and RFC 8247, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why IKEv1 Is Being Retired
sections.content:
IKEv1 and its related documents (ISAKMP in RFC 2408 and the IPsec DOI in RFC 2407, together with RFC 2409) were obsoleted by IKEv2 in RFC 4306 in December 2005. The latest IKEv2 specification at the time of writing was RFC 7296, published in 2014.

The RFC says IKEv2 replaced IKEv1 more than 15 years ago, has seen wide deployment, and is a full replacement for all IKEv1 functionality. No new modifications or algorithms had been accepted for IKEv1 for at least a decade, and IKEv2 fixes problems such as IKEv1 being vulnerable to amplification attacks.
sections.eli5: The newer way of setting up secure connections has been around for a very long time and does everything the old way did. The old way has not been improved in years, so it is time to retire it.

sections.title: RFCs 2407, 2408 and 2409 Are Historic
sections.content:
Systems that run IKEv1 should be upgraded and reconfigured to run IKEv2. The RFC gives several reasons why IKEv1-only systems are poor candidates for continued operation.

  • IKEv1 development ceased over a decade ago, so unmaintained code may hide security vulnerabilities.
  • Some IKEv1 systems have reached End of Life and will never be patched.
  • Some vendors have 'frozen' their IKEv1 implementation, and users may not realise it is unmaintained.
  • IKEv1 systems can be abused for packet amplification attacks, as documented in CVE-2016-5361.
  • The algorithms IKEv1 commonly negotiates are dated, such as AES-CBC, SHA1 and Diffie-Hellman groups 1 or 2.

IKEv2 offers more modern cryptographic primitives, proper defense against denial-of-service attacks, improved authentication through EAP methods, and password-authenticated key exchange (PAKE) support. IKEv2 implementations SHOULD NOT directly import IKEv1 configurations without updating the cryptographic algorithms used.
sections.eli5: Old equipment that nobody fixes can have holes bad guys use. The new system is stronger, so everyone should move over and not just copy the old settings.

sections.title: IKEv1 Features That Moved to IKEv2
sections.content:
A few IKEv1 features are not in the IKEv2 core specification but are available through additional specifications.

  • Post-quantum protection (4.1). IKEv1's use of preshared keys (PSKs) protects against quantum-computer attacks. IKEv2 changed PSK use to improve error reporting, at the expense of post-quantum security. Systems that need it should use IKEv2 Post-quantum Preshared Keys (PPKs) from RFC 8784.
  • Labeled IPsec (4.2). This negotiates an extra Security Context selector for the Security Policy Database, and was never standardized in IKEv1. IKEv2 support is specified in a separate Internet-Draft.
  • Group SAs and multicast (4.3). The Group Domain of Interpretation in RFC 6407 is based on IKEv1. For IKEv2 this work was still in progress as a draft.
sections.eli5: A few special tricks of the old system are not in the main new rulebook. They live in extra booklets, so people who need those tricks should look there.

sections.title: Deprecated Algorithms
sections.content:
RFC 8247 and RFC 8221 avoid recommending broken or weak algorithms, but they leave old, unused ones in a 'MAY be used' state simply by not mentioning them. This RFC deprecates those unmentioned algorithms, which have no known attacks that would have led to earlier deprecation but are no longer advised.

  • Encryption: RC5, IDEA, CAST, Blowfish, and the unspecified 3IDEA, ENCR_DES_IV64 and ENCR_DES_IV32.
  • PRF: the unspecified PRF_HMAC_TIGER.
  • Integrity: HMAC-MD5-128.
  • Diffie-Hellman groups: none.
sections.eli5: Some old tools were never officially banned, only forgotten. This list puts a clear 'please do not use' label on them.

sections.title: Registry Changes at IANA
sections.content:
IANA closed the 'Internet Key Exchange (IKE) Attributes' and 'Magic Numbers for ISAKMP Protocol' registries, noting 'All registries listed below have been closed. See RFC 9395.' Their registration procedures became 'Registry closed'.

IANA also added a Status column to four IKEv2 Transform Type registries: Encryption Algorithm (type 1), Pseudorandom Function (type 2), Integrity Algorithm (type 3) and Key Exchange Method (type 4). Entries from this RFC are marked DEPRECATED (RFC 9395), and a few earlier deprecations are shown as DEPRECATED [RFC8247]. Entries not mentioned receive no value in the new column.
sections.eli5: The list-keepers froze the old notebooks so nothing new can be added, and added a new column to the new notebooks saying which items are no longer recommended.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC states there are only security benefits if IKEv1 is deprecated and IKEv2 is used.

The deprecated algorithms have long been out of use and are no longer actively deployed or researched, which leaves an unknown security risk best avoided. Not supporting them also simplifies implementations and reduces accidental use through misconfiguration or downgrade attacks.
sections.eli5: Fewer old, forgotten tools means fewer ways to trip up or to be tricked into using a weak one.
